name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
title: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
answer: Shadow AI in legal teams is the use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals, and support staff without the approval or visibility of the firm's or legal department's IT and security functions. It covers drafting assistants, summarizers, research chatbots, transcription services, and document analysis tools that employees sign up for on their own, often with personal accounts. The site's index of 732 AI tools gives a sense of how many options a person can reach without asking. The scope includes both deliberate workarounds and accidental use, such as AI features embedded in everyday software that no one flagged. It sits inside AI security audits and enterprise enablement because the response is part discovery, part policy, and part providing a safer alternative.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Shadow AI runs on personal devices, personal cloud accounts, free tiers of public services, browser extensions, and mobile apps, often outside single sign-on and endpoint management. It can also run on work laptops and phones when an employee uses a personal login to a web service that IT does not monitor. Legal teams typically have document management systems, email, and matter management platforms, but shadow AI bypasses those controls and may move client data into environments with no retention or deletion guarantees. Some tools run locally on a laptop, while others send data to public cloud endpoints. The infrastructure is therefore a mix of unmanaged endpoints, consumer accounts, and public model services, which makes discovery and containment difficult.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of auditing and enabling starts with discovery, using network logs, endpoint telemetry, expense reports, browser extension inventories, and interviews with staff about what they actually use. Practitioners then map data flows, classify the risk of each tool, and compare actual use against existing policy. Enablement follows, with approved alternatives that offer enterprise terms, data protection, and logging, plus training that explains why the rules exist. The method is iterative because new tools appear constantly and old ones change their terms. It combines technical scanning with human reporting, since many shadow AI uses leave no clear network signature.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in shadow AI center on client confidentiality, attorney-client privilege, work product protection, data protection law, and intellectual property. When a lawyer pastes client material into an unapproved tool, the firm may lose control over that data, and the tool's terms may allow the provider to use it for training or other purposes. Provenance matters because the firm often cannot say which model produced an output, what data went in, or whether the result is accurate. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows that the legal exposure is real and growing. The site also maintains 219 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting the patchwork of rules that apply across jurisdictions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Shadow AI in legal teams is likely to persist as tools become more capable and more embedded in ordinary software, which blurs the line between sanctioned and unsanctioned use. The site's count of 6947 state AI bills points to a growing compliance burden that legal teams will have to map against their own tool inventories. Expect more continuous monitoring rather than one-time audits, and more pressure to provide approved tools that match the convenience of shadow ones. Vendors are adding AI features to existing platforms, so some shadow use may become sanctioned by default. The direction is toward governance that is embedded in procurement, training, and daily workflow rather than bolted on after the fact.
